newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bluem isolated over German pensions reform.
newsitem.headline: Bluem isolated over German pensions reform.

text.p: Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's longest-serving minister, faces the battle of his career to convince coalition colleagues to back his proposals to reform Germany's pensions system.
Bluem this week unveiled plans to cut old-age pensions, raise contributions and launch a tax-financed "family fund" to keep the compulsory pensions scheme going into the 21st Century.
But he looks to have committed a cardinal error by failing to get all three parties in Kohl's coalition on board, and has even come under fire from fellow Christian Democrats (CDU).
Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf, a senior party figure with a strong track record on welfare policy, called the plan "not serious" and said it would not stand up to scrutiny.
The CDU youth wing was outraged the burden of the changes would fall mainly on young people.
"This is a capitulation over the principle of justice between the generations," Young CDU leader Klaus Escher said.

A commission of experts under pugnacious Bluem on Monday proposed a scheme which would keep the existing system intact and ruled out radical reforms like boosting capital reserves in the pay-as-you-go system.
Analysts say a big pensions shakeup would stir up too much resistance from those who would lose out. But too little change now would force more stop-gap action in a few years.

"It is simply too late for fundamental reforms which pose huge transitional problems and run the risk of numerous inequities and even hardship," Hans Jaeckel, DG Bank's head of domestic economic research, wrote in a commentary for Reuters.
To prevent the "greying" of the German population from overburdening the system, Bluem proposed cutting pensions to 64 percent of average net wages by 2030 from 70 percent now.
Pension contributions, which were hiked this year to a record 20.3 percent of wages, would have to rise again to 22.9 percent over the same period.
The daily Die Welt wrote that, despite months of preparatory work, Bluem's commission had failed to deliver a convincing reform concept.
"The only people who will be happy are today's pensioners, who barely lose out," it wrote. "Those paying contributions and future pensioners, on the contrary, face uncertainty."
Bluem also wants a two-point increase in value-added taxes to pay for some non-related items currently borne by pension charges, such as child benefits.
"One percent on VAT for the tax reform and one percent for pensions," Bluem said in an interview in Stern magazine.

But that has been rejected by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who is simultaneously trying to push through cuts in direct and indirect taxes worth 30 billion marks ($18 billion) to boost investment and put Germany's four million jobless back to work.
Bluem reportedly threatened to resign last week over Waigel's plan to raise taxes on pensions -- one of 70 proposals to scrap exemptions seen as skewing the German tax system.

But Waigel is on firmer ground. Although his tax plans have met hostility from the opposition, trade unions and other lobbies, he won the support of all three government parties by involving them in the policy drafting process.

The coalition is split, however, over pensions. Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) -- the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's CDU -- and the Free Democrats (FDP) joined in attacking Bluem's pensions strategy.
CSU parliamentary leader Michael Glos on Tuesday called the reform proposal merely "a contribution to the debate". The CSU opposes Bluem's family fund idea.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the FDP, went further, saying: "Herr Bluem's proposal is not government policy, and cannot become government policy."
Westerwelle said on Wednesday the FDP would draft its own pensions proposals.

Commentators in Bonn said that if Bluem -- the only minister to have voted against Waigel's tax plan -- were to quit it would be a serious blow to Kohl, who has had to quell rare attacks from up-and-coming CDU leaders over the tax reforms.

The 66-year-old chancellor has not said publicly whether he will run for a record fifth term in 1998. But his crown prince, CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, has already stoked speculation that he is ready to take over the helm. ($1=1.6405 Mark)
